presentingComplaint: 6 weeks of worsening lower back pain, fatigue and rising creatinine noted at his diabetes clinic.
history: Retired schoolteacher with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine ~1.6 mg/dL) presents with 6 weeks of progressively severe, band-like lower thoracolumbar back pain that is worse at night and no longer relieved by paracetamol. Over the same period he reports profound fatigue, anorexia, roughly 5 kg unintentional weight loss, constipation, polyuria and increasing thirst which he initially attributed to poor glycaemic control. His GP found the creatinine had climbed from 1.6 to 3.1 mg/dL and referred him. He denies fever, dysuria, cough or melaena. He has had two 'chest colds' this winter. Medications: metformin, gliclazide, ramipril, atorvastatin. No NSAID use. Ex-smoker (20 pack-years), minimal alcohol.
examination: Elderly man, alert but tired-looking and clinically dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Conjunctival pallor present. No jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly. Marked tenderness over the mid-lumbar spinous processes with paraspinal spasm; power and reflexes intact in lower limbs with no sensory level and normal perianal sensation. Chest clear, heart sounds normal, no peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal neurological deficit.

labs.SPEP: monoclonal (M) band in gamma region, IgG kappa on immunofixation, ~42 g/L
labs.urine: Bence-Jones protein positive; dipstick trace protein only (albumin-insensitive to light chains)

imaging: Whole-body low-dose CT: multiple well-defined lytic (punched-out) lesions in the calvarium, several vertebral bodies and both proximal femora, with a wedge compression of L2 and no retropulsion or cord compromise. No sclerotic metastatic pattern.
microbiology: Not applicable - no evidence of active infection; blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Multiple myeloma (CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, lytic bone lesions)
Acute-on-chronic kidney injury from another cause (e.g., cast nephropathy vs volume depletion)
Metastatic carcinoma with bony deposits (e.g., prostate, lung)
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy from a solid tumour
finalDiagnosis: Symptomatic multiple myeloma (IgG kappa) presenting with CRAB criteria - hypercalcaemia, renal impairment (cast nephropathy superimposed on diabetic CKD), anaemia and lytic bone disease.
citations: IMWG (International Myeloma Working Group) - Updated Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Myeloma, 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition - Plasma Cell Disorders
stewardship: Non-infective presentation - no antimicrobial therapy indicated. Emphasis is on recognising the myeloma-defining CRAB features rather than attributing the rising creatinine and symptoms to the patient's diabetes and CKD. Avoid nephrotoxic insults (hold ACE inhibitor, avoid iodinated contrast and NSAIDs), correct hypercalcaemia with IV isotonic saline rehydration and consider bisphosphonate/denosumab with renal dosing, and refer urgently to haematology for confirmatory bone marrow biopsy (clonal plasma cells) and systemic anti-myeloma therapy.
contraindications: Avoid NSAIDs and iodinated contrast in the setting of light-chain cast nephropathy and CKD
Hold ACE inhibitor (ramipril) during acute kidney injury and hypercalcaemia
Do not give IV bisphosphonate without renal dose adjustment and adequate rehydration
Avoid loop diuretics for hypercalcaemia until euvolaemic (worsens dehydration)
edgeCases: Widened globulin gap and heavy Bence-Jones proteinuria with only trace dipstick protein are easily missed if renal decline is blamed on diabetic nephropathy
Corrected calcium must be used given the low albumin, otherwise hypercalcaemia is underestimated
Rouleaux and a very high ESR are clues even before the paraprotein is identified
expectedMaiK: Recognise the CRAB tetrad (hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lytic lesions) in an elderly diabetic/CKD patient and pursue serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains rather than attributing the picture to diabetic nephropathy.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the back pain worse at night/at rest, and are there any red-flag neurological symptoms (leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction)?
Has there been recent unexplained weight loss, recurrent infections or bone pain elsewhere?
What is the trajectory of the creatinine relative to the diabetic/CKD baseline, and any recent NSAID or contrast exposure?
Any symptoms of hypercalcaemia - thirst, polyuria, constipation, confusion?
expectedInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light-chain assay
Corrected serum calcium, renal profile and albumin
Full blood count with peripheral smear (rouleaux)
24h urine / spot urine for Bence-Jones protein (urine immunofixation)
Whole-body low-dose CT or MRI for lytic lesions and to exclude cord compression
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for clonal plasma cell percentage
Beta-2 microglobulin and LDH for staging (R-ISS)

investigations: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
Whole-body low-dose CT or MRI skeletal survey

regressionAssertions: Engine must return myeloma as the top diagnosis given widened globulin gap, monoclonal band, hypercalcaemia, anaemia and lytic bone lesions
Must not attribute the acute rise in creatinine solely to diabetic nephropathy/CKD
Must recommend SPEP/immunofixation and serum free light chains as key investigations
Must not recommend empiric antibiotics (non-infective presentation)
Must flag hypercalcaemia management with IV fluids and avoidance of nephrotoxins
